title: 4 Steps to Set Up No-Code Automation + Workflow Examples
summary: No code automation platforms can handle your workflows at different price points. Find which of 7 options fits your team's technical level and budget.
body_markdown:
## 4. Activepieces: best for open source and AI agents


If your team has the technical skill to run its own tooling, Activepieces suits it. It's an automation platform whose core is **MIT-licensed, so you can self-host it** or use the vendor's cloud.


Connectors are called "pieces," and they're open code you can read and extend. The enterprise directories (` packages/ee/` ) sit under a separate commercial licence, stated in the LICENSE file of the activepieces/activepieces repository, and everything released under MIT is yours to run, fork, resell or embed.


That's the difference from n8n's fair-code terms, and it means a renewal increase or a paywalled feature never forces you to migrate on a vendor's schedule. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


If you want the workflow builder of a no-code tool but need the data to stay on your own infrastructure, this fits.


It also fits teams building AI agents that call tools, including through MCP (Model Context Protocol, the standard that lets an agent discover and use external tools). Someone still has to own upgrades, backups and uptime if you self-host.


You pay nothing in licence fees for the self-hosted community edition; the servers and the engineer's time are the cost instead.


The cloud and enterprise tiers are paid. I have no confirmed figures to quote, so read the vendor's pricing page for current limits. Ask in particular whether usage is metered per task or per flow run, because that decides how the bill grows.


Because the core is open, you can inspect what a connector does with your credentials, and you can write a missing one yourself instead of waiting on a vendor roadmap.


Self-hosting removes per-task metering, which is the billing edge case that makes high-volume workflows expensive on hosted platforms.


The AI-agent and MCP support is built into the product rather than bolted on.


Breadth is the trade-off. The three platforms with published counts show how wide the field is:


Against Zapier's 9,000 apps, Make's 3,500+ and n8n's 2,368 (13 October 2026), Activepieces sits in the smaller tier, so a niche line-of-business app may have no integration, and you'd have to build it or call its API directly.


That gap matters most when your stack includes obscure tools, and the integrations directory is the first thing to check. The community is also smaller than Zapier's, so fewer ready-made templates and tutorials exist.


Choose Zapier if nobody on the team wants to maintain infrastructure and your apps are mainstream. Choose Make if your difficulty is branching, iterators and data mapping that you want to see on a canvas.


Choose n8n if you need self-hosting and deeper code nodes, and can accept its source-available licence rather than a pure MIT one.
